analysis.one_liner: Charges a fee on fossil fuel carbon pollution and returns the money to workers, retirees, and states.
analysis.headline: The carbon fee bill was introduced in February 2018, referred to five House committees, and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would put a fee on the carbon dioxide released by coal, oil, and natural gas — plus fluorinated gases and methane leaked from fuel supply chains — starting at $50 per ton in 2019 and rising until U.S. emissions fall to 20 percent of their 2005 level. The money would go back to the public: a tax credit of up to $800 per worker ($1,600 for couples), equivalent payments to Social Security beneficiaries, veterans, and disabled Americans, and $10 billion a year in grants to states to help low-income and rural households with energy costs and to retrain fossil fuel workers. It would also refund the fee for exports and captured carbon, protect energy-intensive manufacturers with border adjustments, and cut the corporate income tax rate. The bill was referred to five House committees and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Working people would benefit directly: every worker would get a refundable tax credit of up to $800 per year ($1,600 for married couples), while retirees, veterans, and disabled Americans who don't owe income tax would get an equivalent check each year. Low-income households would get extra monthly rebates through their states, and fossil fuel workers would get priority for retraining and transition help. Future generations benefit from the emissions cuts, and energy-intensive manufacturers would be protected from foreign competitors through border adjustments. The bill also cuts the corporate income tax rate, a direct gain for corporations and their shareholders.

how_it_helps.text: Working people would receive a refundable tax credit of up to $800 per year ($1,600 for joint filers), adjusted for inflation, to offset the higher energy prices the fee causes.
Social Security beneficiaries, veterans, and disabled Americans who do not file for the credit would receive an equivalent annual payment instead.
Low-income and rural households would get additional help through a $10 billion-per-year state grant program, including monthly household rebates for people near the poverty line.
Coal, oil, and gas workers would get priority for job training and transition assistance as fossil fuel employment shrinks.
The fee would rise over time until U.S. greenhouse gas emissions fall to 20 percent of their 2005 level, targeting the emissions driving climate change.

analysis.who_pays: Fossil fuel producers, utilities, and ultimately energy consumers would pay the carbon fee, built into the price of gasoline, heating fuel, and electricity. Energy-intensive manufacturers would face higher input costs, though export refunds and border adjustments soften that. Corporations would pay a carbon fee but recoup some of it through the lower corporate tax rate.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil fuel producers and energy consumers

drawbacks.text: The fee would raise the price of gasoline, heating fuel, and electricity, which falls hardest on households that drive long distances or heat with oil or gas — the bill tries to offset this with a credit of at most $800 per worker ($1,600 per couple), which may not cover the added costs for some families.

The bill reduces the corporate income tax rate as part of the package (per its stated purpose), returning some of the carbon revenue to corporations and shareholders rather than entirely to households.

The bill leans on administrative complexity — Treasury-determined fees on supply-chain methane leakage, lists of 'energy-intensive manufactured goods,' and state-by-state rebate programs — creating many places where implementation could falter or favor incumbent industries.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core design is economically sound in the way economists across the spectrum generally favor: charge polluters the real cost of their emissions, return the money to households so most working people come out ahead, and shield energy-intensive manufacturers with border adjustments so jobs don't simply move overseas. The offsets are capped (up to $800 per worker, twice for couples), which could leave heavy energy users — rural drivers, homes heated with fuel oil — worse off despite the state grants; the bill itself acknowledges this by funding household rebates for low-income families. The corporate rate cut paired with it gives back some of the revenue to shareholders rather than households. But the biggest weakness is that none of it was ever seriously considered: the bill died in committee with one cosponsor and no hearing or vote.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to five House committees in February 2018 and never advanced — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Representative Earl Blumenauer introduced the bill on February 5, 2018, with Representative David Cicilline as the only cosponsor.
The House referred it to the Ways and Means Committee and four others: Transportation and Infrastructure, Veterans' Affairs, Energy and Commerce, and Education and the Workforce.

Two subcommittees received referrals — Railroads, Pipelines, and Hazardous Materials (February 2018) and Higher Education and Workforce Development (April 2018) — but no committee ever took further action.
No vote was ever held in either chamber; all House action after introduction was referrals, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel producers and major emitters, who avoided a rising carbon fee, and corporations, which kept the corporate tax rate the bill would have lowered in exchange. Workers and retirees lost the offset payments and state assistance the bill would have funded.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel producers and major emitters

for.name: Rep. Earl Blumenauer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and wrote its carbon fee and dividend framework.

for.name: Rep. David Cicilline
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as its only cosponsor.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no report.

against.name: House leadership of the 115th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor for a vote; no further action appears in the record after subcommittee referrals.

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and with Republicans controlling the House, the bill never advanced in any committee.

industries.industry: Coal, oil, and natural gas producers
industries.note: The bill charges these industries a rising fee per ton of carbon dioxide — starting at $50 — plus a supplement for methane leaked and vented across their supply chains, directly reducing demand for their products. It does offer refunds for captured carbon and exports.

industries.industry: Fossil fuel consumers (utilities, refiners, energy-intensive manufacturers)
industries.note: They would pay the fee on fossil fuels they buy, but the bill refunds the fee for exported products and for goods whose carbon is captured, and border adjustments protect manufacturers competing against imports.
Companies that capture and securely store or reuse carbon dioxide from fossil fuel use get a full refund of the fee, creating a paid incentive for capture technology.
By making coal, oil, and gas steadily more expensive relative to wind, solar, and efficiency, the fee shifts energy investment toward lower-emission sources.
